segments.title: Management is more than common sense
segments.script: So, you're in this course and you may have pondered, or discussed with others, what this course will be about. You probably have some preconceptions of what management is all about. You must manage your time, deciding on how much study time you will devote to your management and accounting classes, for instance. You may have had a summer or part-time job where you had a manager whom you had to report to. You may have followed news reports on successful managers like Jeff Bezos of Amazon or Sheryl Sandberg of Facebook and want to learn what made them successful so you can emulate their practices in your business career. You may have the impression (not an accurate one) that management is basically just common sense and that you really don't need to take this course except that you must meet your degree requirement. You may be an accounting or marketing major who is taking this class because it is required for completion of your degree requirements, but you don't think that you will ever require what you learn in this class during your career since you don't plan on applying for HR jobs upon graduation. If you're believing this, you could not be more mistaken. Regardless of where you are in your career, be it as an individual contributor, project leader, or middle or senior manager, what you will get out of this course will be valuable. If your first job out of college is as an accountant, sales representative, or another entry-level position, you will appreciate the roles that your managers, both direct and senior level, play in an organization and the behaviors and actions that will get you recognized and appreciated. Best of luck! Most management textbooks would say, as does this one, that managers spend their time engaged in planning, organizing, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting, and controlling. These activities, as Hannaway found in her study of managers at work, "do not, in fact, describe what managers do." At best they seem to describe vague objectives that managers are continually trying to accomplish. The real world, however, is far from being that simple. The world in which most managers work is a "messy and hectic stream of ongoing activity."
keyPoints: What you learn about management is useful at every career stage, not only in HR or senior jobs
Textbooks list planning, organizing, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and controlling
Hannaway found those activities do not describe what managers actually do
Real managerial work is a messy and hectic stream of ongoing activity
segments.altExplanation: The textbook list of management activities reads like a tidy job description. When researchers watched managers at work, the tidy list did not match what they saw. The list describes goals managers keep aiming at, while the day itself is messy, hectic and continuous.
segments.deeper: The chapter's learning objectives frame the whole course: what managers do to help organizations achieve top performance, the roles they play, and the characteristics effective managers display. The rest of this chapter answers each of those in turn.

checkpoint.prompt: According to Hannaway, what is wrong with the textbook list of planning, organizing and controlling?
options: It leaves out reporting and budgeting
It does not describe what managers actually do
It only applies to senior managers in big firms
checkpoint.answer: It does not describe what managers actually do
checkpoint.rubric: Hannaway found that these activities "do not, in fact, describe what managers do"; at best they describe vague objectives managers keep trying to reach.

checkpoint.prompt: How does the chapter describe the world most managers actually work in?
checkpoint.answer: A messy and hectic stream of ongoing activity.
checkpoint.rubric: Must convey that managerial work is messy, hectic or a constant stream of activity rather than a neat, orderly process.
